summary: Campaign just started. The codebase (2,800 lines, zero dependencies) was surveyed end-to-end and a reproducible benchmark harness now lives in perf/. Baseline numbers are recorded below; two implementation lanes are being dispatched in parallel worktrees: CPU/library (EPUB zip writer, page-blob decode, manifest hashing) and network/interface (HTTP connection reuse, concurrent downloads).

Measured headline opportunities at baseline: CRC32 done in a pure-JS byte loop where Node ships a native one (~70× on 4 MB); every JPEG asset is run through deflate level 9 although random-byte data compresses 0% at any level; all HTTP requests pay a fresh TLS handshake (no keep-alive pooling on the secure path); audiobook parts, magazine pages, and page assets are all downloaded strictly one-at-a-time.

waves.name: Native CRC32 in the EPUB zip writer
waves.change: Replace the 256-entry-table pure-JS CRC32 loop in src/epub.mjs with Node's native zlib.crc32 (available since Node 20.15).
tradeoffs: engines floor must move from >=20 to >=20.15 (applied at integration)
CRC result verified byte-identical by the bench

waves.name: Store already-compressed media instead of deflating
waves.change: zip() runs deflate level 9 over every entry. JPEG/PNG/GIF/webp/MP3/PDF payloads compress 0% (measured ratio 1.000 at levels 6 and 9) — store them uncompressed like the mimetype entry already is.
tradeoffs: If a file were mislabeled (e.g. a .jpg that is actually uncompressed), the EPUB would carry it raw — size grows by that file's compression potential. In practice scan assets are real JPEGs.
EPUB readers accept stored entries (spec-compliant); verified with unzip -t at integration.

waves.name: Deflate level 9 → 6 for compressible entries
waves.change: For text/XHTML entries, level 6 is 2× faster than level 9 for a 0.088 → 0.090 ratio (+2% on the text portion, <0.1% of a real EPUB's bytes since image scans dominate).
tradeoffs: EPUB files grow ~2% on their text entries; total archive size impact is well under 1% because image assets dominate.
Reversible one-liner if the owner prefers level 9.

waves.name: Single-allocation zip assembly (peak RAM)
waves.change: zip() accumulates every entry in a chunk list, then Buffer.concat copies the whole EPUB a second time. Building directly into one preallocated output buffer removes that copy.
tradeoffs: Compressed entries still exist transiently (deflate cannot target an existing buffer synchronously); a full streaming zip-to-file would cut peak further but changes the public API — deferred unless the owner wants it.

waves.name: Faster __bif_cfc1 page-blob decode
waves.change: read.mjs deciphers every read-host page with a regex replace over the blob (per-match overhead at MB scale). Replace with a semantics-identical code-unit swap loop.
tradeoffs: Must replicate regex '．' semantics (groups spanning line terminators are left intact) — equivalence asserted by the bench.

waves.name: Parallel integrity-manifest hashing
waves.change: writeManifest() hashes every archived file one stream at a time. Hash up to ~8 files concurrently (order preserved in the output manifest).
tradeoffs: More concurrent file handles during the final pass (bounded, closed when done). Manifest content must stay byte-identical — asserted by the bench.

waves.name: Keep-alive HTTP connection pooling
waves.change: jsonRequest/fetchBuffer use the default global agent (keepAlive off): every Thunder/stargazer/cover call pays a full TLS handshake. Pool connections per host with a bounded keep-alive agent while keeping the per-request socket timeouts that guard against the historic wedge failure.
tradeoffs: Sockets linger open briefly after the last request (bounded by keep-alive TTL); CLI exit closes them.
Must keep per-request timeouts — a pooled agent without them is exactly the failure mode the http.mjs header comment warns about.

waves.name: Concurrent audiobook part downloads
waves.change: archive.mjs downloads spine parts strictly sequentially. Fetch 3 parts at a time (bounded), preserving per-part resume/skip logic and logs.
tradeoffs: 3 simultaneous connections to the OverDrive CDN per title — politeness bound kept low on purpose.
Failure of one part still aborts the loan; resume logic unchanged.

waves.name: Concurrent page + asset fetching (ebooks/magazines)
waves.change: archive-read.mjs fetches and decodes pages one at a time (a 300-page magazine = 300 serial round trips), then assets one at a time. Bound concurrency at 4, preserving spine order for EPUB assembly and fail-fast on first error.
tradeoffs: In-flight page/asset bodies raise steady-state RAM by the concurrency factor (a few MB); bounded at 4.
Bursts of 4 parallel requests to the read host with the session cookie — same host the browser uses.

waves.name: CLI lazy command loading
waves.change: Considered splitting bin/libby.mjs imports per command. Measured first: full import graph costs ~9 ms over the bare Node floor (36.4 vs 27.3 ms for `libby help`).
tradeoffs: Rejected: ≤9 ms upside is invisible next to process spawn cost, and dynamic imports move load errors from startup to command time. Recorded so nobody re-litigates it.

adoption: Nothing on main changes during the trial. Work happens on branches perf-trial-20260906-030748 (integration) with per-lane branches, all created from be863fd.
When the trial is accepted, the hub branch fast-forwards or is cherry-picked into main; each wave is an independent commit so any piece can be adopted or dropped alone.
